newsitem.title: USA: CIA chief won't push death for alleged turncoat.
newsitem.headline: CIA chief won't push death for alleged turncoat.

text.p: CIA Director John Deutch said on Tuesday that he would back a government decision not to seek the death penalty if a former CIA station chief is convicted of selling an unknown quantity of secrets to Russia.
"That's a decision for the prosecutor and I would stand with the prosecutor's decision," Deutch said in a joint appearance on the NBC "Today" programme with FBI Director Louis Freeh.

Prosecutors said on Monday that Harold Nicholson, the highest ranking Central Intelligence Agency officer ever charged with spying, faced life imprisonment without possibility of parole if convicted on the basis of the evidence they now have.

The government alleged that for the past two years Nicholson gave Moscow information identifying U.S. spies about to be sent abroad, among other secrets, in exchange for cash payments totalling at least $120,000.

Deutch said Nicholson, 46, had been detected and brought to justice about as quickly as possible thanks to what he and Freeh hailed as seemless cooperation between the CIA and the Federal Bureau of Investigation, which have frequently fought turf battles in the past.

Deutch contrasted the two-year period during which Nicholson allegedly sold secrets to Moscow with the nearly 10 years that convicted CIA turncoat Aldrich Ames betrayed U.S. agents under the CIA's nose.
"It's quite an accomplishment and I think just about as much as one could expect in these very difficult cases," Deutch said.
"We're stronger now than we were during the Cold War in my view to enforce the counter-intelligence programme, and I think the rapidity of this (Nichoslon) case...is good proof of that," Freeh added.
Nicholson, 46, was a 16-year clandestine operations officer who was CIA station chief in Romania and deputy chief of station in Malaysia before becoming a CIA instructor in intelligence tradecraft.
